title: How to file a motor insurance claim in Kenya: a step-by-step guide
excerpt: Most motor claim delays in Kenya trace back to missing documents and late notification — not insurer unwillingness to pay. This guide covers what to do at the scene, what to submit on day one, and how your broker can help you avoid a back-and-forth file.
author: ADT Motor Risk Team
content: A motor incident is stressful. The difference between a claim that moves in days and one that stalls for weeks usually comes down to what you capture in the first hour and what you submit in the first 24 hours. Kenyan motor policies typically require prompt notification, accurate facts, and supporting documents that match your policy wording.
## Step 1: Secure the scene and notify immediately

Once everyone is safe, call emergency services if needed and notify the police where the incident is reportable. Contact your broker or insurer as soon as practical — many policies expect notification within 24 to 48 hours. Have your policy number, vehicle registration, and a clear summary of what happened ready.
- Note exact time, date, and location (landmark, road name, or GPS pin)
- Record names, phone numbers, and vehicle details for all parties involved
- Do not admit fault at the scene; stick to factual statements
- Ask witnesses for contact details if third-party liability may be involved
## Step 2: Document damage before anything moves

Insurers assess what they can see in your evidence. Take wide shots of the scene and close-ups of all damaged panels, tyres, lights, and interior items. Photograph number plates, licence discs, and any debris on the road.
- Capture all four sides of your vehicle and any third-party vehicles
- Photograph the road layout, traffic signs, and skid marks if visible
- Keep originals of your driving licence, ID, and logbook accessible for copies
- If the vehicle is drivable, photograph damage again at a repair yard before dismantling
## Step 3: Obtain the police abstract and complete the claim form

For many motor claims in Kenya, a police abstract (OB number) is required. Request it promptly and confirm the facts match your incident report. Complete the insurer claim form accurately — inconsistencies between the abstract, your statement, and repair estimates are a common cause of delay.
- Match dates, times, and locations across every document
- Attach two or three repair estimates from reputable garages if repairs are needed
- Include towing receipts if the vehicle was recovered from the scene
- Submit third-party details and witness statements where liability is disputed
## Step 4: Work with your broker before formal submission

Your broker reviews files daily and knows what each insurer expects on first submission. ADT can pre-check your bundle on WhatsApp or email, flag missing items, and escalate to the claims desk when urgency matters — for example fleet downtime or hire-purchase financier requirements.
- Ask your advisor which documents are mandatory for your cover type (comprehensive vs third party)
- Confirm whether the insurer wants digital submission, physical forms, or both
- Keep one internal contact for all insurer follow-up to avoid conflicting instructions
- Track reference numbers and assessment appointments in writing
## What slows motor claims down — and how to avoid it

Late notification without explanation, blurry photos, repair estimates that do not match the damage described, and missing financier letters are frequent hold-ups. If you could not report immediately because of hospitalisation or remote location, document the reason and the date you first informed your broker.

ADT's motor team supports private, commercial, and fleet clients across Kenya. If you are unsure what your policy requires after an incident, contact the claims desk before you authorise repairs or dispose of damaged parts.

title: WIBA explained: who is legally required to have it and what it covers
excerpt: Work Injury Benefits Act cover is mandatory for Kenyan employers — yet many businesses still carry outdated employee schedules or confuse WIBA with optional employers liability. This guide explains who must comply, what benefits employees receive, and how to structure cover without gaps at renewal.
author: ADT Compliance Desk
content: The Work Injury Benefits Act (WIBA) establishes compulsory insurance for employers against liability for work-related injuries, occupational diseases, and death arising from employment. If you employ staff in Kenya — even a small team — WIBA compliance is not optional. Operating without valid cover exposes the business to penalties and leaves employees without the statutory benefits they are entitled to.
## Who must have WIBA cover?

Employers with one or more employees engaged under a contract of service are generally required to maintain WIBA-compliant insurance. This applies across sectors: retail, construction, logistics, hospitality, manufacturing, and professional services with support staff. Casual, temporary, and part-time workers should be reflected accurately on your policy schedule — under-declaring headcount is a common renewal problem.
- Confirm all employees on payroll are listed with correct IDs and job roles
- Include new hires before they start hazardous duties where possible
- Review contractor arrangements separately — true contractors may fall outside WIBA, but misclassification creates risk
- Align cover with DOSH reporting obligations for serious injuries
## What does WIBA pay when an injury happens?

WIBA provides defined benefits for medical expenses, temporary or permanent disability, and death benefits to dependants where a work-related injury or disease occurs. The scheme is designed to compensate employees without forcing every case through lengthy civil litigation. Benefit levels and procedures are set in law and policy wording — your broker should explain how claims are filed and what documentation the insurer expects.
- Medical treatment costs related to the work injury
- Compensation for temporary total or partial disablement
- Lump-sum or pension-style benefits for permanent disablement
- Death benefits payable to dependants where a fatality arises from employment
## WIBA vs employers liability — do you need both?

WIBA is statutory and mandatory. Employers liability (EL) cover addresses broader legal liability to employees beyond the WIBA schedule — for example certain negligence claims. Many corporates carry both. SMEs sometimes assume WIBA alone covers every workforce incident; your advisor should map operational risks (machinery, driving duties, height work) against both policies.
## Staying compliant at renewal without overpaying
Premiums are driven by employee numbers, industry classification, claims history, and salary roll where applicable. Accurate data is the best way to avoid surprise premium jumps or rejected claims.
- Reconcile HR records with the policy schedule 30 days before expiry
- Declare changes in turnover, new sites, or shift patterns that affect risk
- Investigate near-misses and minor injuries — they predict future claims
- Keep induction records and safety training logs for audit readiness

ADT structures WIBA for businesses from single-site SMEs to multi-location corporates. If you are unsure whether your current certificate matches your actual workforce, request a compliance review before your next renewal.

title: Five ways SMEs can reduce insurance claim delays
excerpt: SME owners often discover — at the worst moment — that nobody knows where the policy schedule is, photos were never taken, or the incident was reported a week late. These five habits reduce insurer back-and-forth and keep cash flow stable after a loss.
author: ADT Advisory Desk
content: Small and medium enterprises feel claim delays more sharply than large corporates: stock loss, vehicle downtime, or property damage directly affects payroll and supplier payments. In our experience, delays are rarely caused by insurers refusing to act — they happen when the first submission is incomplete, facts are inconsistent, or nobody owns the file internally.
## 1. Assign one claims contact before an incident happens

Choose a single person — owner, operations lead, or finance manager — who is authorised to speak to your broker and insurer. Share their name and mobile number with ADT and store it with your policy documents. Multiple conflicting contacts slow decisions.
- Publish the claims contact on your staff noticeboard or operations manual
- Give them access to policy numbers, schedules, and past renewal correspondence
- Brief a deputy for nights, weekends, and travel periods
## 2. Build a simple incident folder you can grab in minutes
Keep digital and physical copies of active policies, payment receipts, asset registers, and key invoices. After fire, theft, or flood, searching for paperwork adds days.
- Store policies and schedules in cloud storage with offline backup
- Maintain a photo register of premises, stock rooms, and high-value equipment
- Keep supplier invoices for major stock purchases dated within the last year
## 3. Report within 24 hours even if details are incomplete
You can supplement documents later, but late notification triggers questions about cover. Call or WhatsApp your broker with what you know: what happened, when, where, and what is damaged.
- Send first photos from your phone the same day
- State clearly if police, fire brigade, or hospital attendance occurred
- Note what you are still gathering and when you will follow up
## 4. Use a one-page checklist for every incident type
Motor, burglary, fire, goods in transit, and WIBA injuries each need different documents. ADT provides checklists in the document centre — print one per branch or save them to your phone.
- Motor: photos, abstract, licence, logbook, estimates
- Burglary: photos, inventory loss list, alarm records, police report
- Fire: photos, fire brigade report, damage inventory, repair quotes
## 5. Pre-agree escalation with your broker

SMEs without a risk department rely on brokers for triage. Ask ADT for named claims desk contacts and expected response times during business hours. For fleet or stock-critical incidents, escalate early rather than waiting for the insurer to request more papers.

Implementing these habits takes one afternoon of setup and saves weeks when a claim actually happens. Request an SME risk review if you want help aligning policies to how your business really operates.

title: Marine insurance for importers and exporters: what to know
excerpt: Cargo through the Port of Mombasa and East African corridors faces port handling risks, inland transit gaps, and documentation mismatches that standard policies miss. This guide explains marine cover types, Incoterms, and the evidence you need before and after shipment.
author: ADT Corporate Risk Desk
content: Marine cargo insurance protects goods against physical loss or damage while in transit — typically by sea, air, or connected inland carriage. For Kenyan importers and exporters, the journey often includes multiple handlers: overseas port, vessel or air carrier, Mombasa clearance, warehousing, and last-mile delivery. Each handoff is a point where damage, theft, or shortage can occur.
## Types of marine cover importers should understand

Policies are often arranged on Institute Cargo Clauses (A), (B), or (C) — with (A) providing the broadest cover and (C) the most restricted. Your sales contract and Incoterms determine who is responsible for arranging insurance and at what point risk transfers. Misalignment between contract, Incoterm, and actual policy is a leading cause of uninsured losses.
- Clause A: generally all-risks subject to policy exclusions
- Clause B: named perils plus specified accidental causes
- Clause C: restricted cover — often unsuitable for high-value or fragile cargo
- Contingency or seller's interest cover when buyers arrange insurance but you retain risk
## Align cover with Incoterms and consignment value

If you sell FOB Mombasa but your buyer's insurance starts overseas, clarify who covers the inland leg to the port. If you buy CIF, verify the seller's policy actually names your interest and covers the full invoice value including freight and duty where needed.
- Insure for full replacement value, not only invoice minimums
- Declare currency and exchange rate assumptions on high-value shipments
- Add war and strikes clauses where routes justify them
- Review exclusions for improper packing, delay, and inherent vice
## Documentation that speeds claims at Mombasa
When cargo arrives damaged or short, the clock starts immediately. Notify your broker before removing goods from the port or carrier custody where possible, and arrange survey if required.
- Commercial invoice and packing list matching quantities received
- Bill of lading or air waybill with clean or claused remarks noted
- Delivery notes, gate passes, and warehouse receipts
- Photos of external packaging and internal damage before repacking
- Shortage or damage report lodged with carrier or port within time limits
## Inland transit and warehouse gaps

Many losses happen after discharge — during trucking to Nairobi, Eldoret, or regional borders. Extend cover to include inland transit and storage if your operations need it. Single-transit policies that end at the port leave SMEs exposed every day.

ADT advises importers, exporters, and logistics firms on marine structures tied to real shipping patterns through Mombasa and regional corridors. Request a review before your next high-value consignment or annual policy renewal.

title: Group vs individual medical cover: which makes sense for your business?
excerpt: Group medical plans can cut per-person cost significantly — but minimum membership rules, provider networks, and sub-limits trip up growing teams. Compare group and individual structures before you commit at renewal or hire your tenth employee.
author: ADT Health Benefits Team
content: Medical insurance is often the benefit employees value most. For Kenyan businesses, the choice is rarely only "cheapest premium" — it is whether group underwriting, network access, and dependant rules fit your team size, budget, and retention goals. Individual and family plans remain important for owners, contractors, and staff not yet on a corporate scheme.
## When group medical cover makes sense

Group plans pool risk across members, which usually improves per-person pricing above minimum membership thresholds — often from as few as 5 to 10 lives depending on insurer. They suit employers offering inpatient, outpatient, maternity, dental, or optical benefits as a standard package.
- You have stable headcount and predictable annual renewal
- You want one insurer relationship and consolidated billing
- You need dependant cover rules applied consistently across staff
- You can commit to anti-selection controls (waiting periods, disclosures)
## When individual or family plans are better

Founders, directors, and freelancers may prefer individual policies tailored to their age, dependants, and preferred hospitals. Some insurers offer richer chronic disease programmes on retail plans. Teams below group minimums often combine individual cover for key people with a staged plan to migrate to group as headcount grows.
- Part-time or seasonal staff who do not fit group eligibility
- Senior hires who want specific hospital networks
- Staff already covered on a spouse's employer scheme
## Compare more than the headline premium
Two quotes with similar annual cost can perform very differently at claim time. Review the benefit schedule line by line with your broker.
- Inpatient and outpatient annual limits and sub-limits per condition
- Co-payments, room bands, and pre-authorisation rules
- Maternity waiting periods and dependant age caps
- Chronic condition cover, HIV programmes, and cancer caps
- Panel vs non-panel provider reimbursement rates
## Designing a structure that scales with your team

Growing SMEs often start with a mid-tier group plan and add executive top-up or individual plans for leadership. Corporaates may layer group base cover with outpatient-only schemes for certain cadres. ADT maps provider networks in Mombasa, Nairobi, and regional cities to where your staff actually live and work.

Before renewal, run a utilisation review: which benefits were used, which sub-limits were hit, and whether network hospitals matched employee needs. That data drives a smarter group vs individual decision than premium alone.

title: Pre-renewal checklist for corporate insurance buyers
excerpt: Corporate renewals fail quietly: new warehouses uninsured, liability limits unchanged since pre-pandemic revenue, or WIBA schedules still listing last year's headcount. Use this checklist in the 90 days before expiry to close gaps before the board asks.
author: ADT Corporate Risk Desk
content: Corporate insurance programmes span property, liability, motor fleets, marine, medical, WIBA, cyber, and specialty lines — often with different expiry dates and insurers. Renewal season is when silent underinsurance surfaces: assets added without endorsement, contracts requiring higher limits, or claims trends that should have triggered cover changes mid-year.
## Risk register vs policy schedule

Start by comparing your enterprise risk register to active policies. Every material location, subsidiary, and activity should map to a cover line. If operations changed — new depot, outsourced logistics, e-commerce warehouse — flag it before the insurer issues a renewal invite.
- List all owned and leased premises with values and occupancy
- Note new countries, agents, or joint ventures affecting liability
- Identify capital projects, machinery, and IT assets added in the last 12 months
- Record contracts requiring minimum insurance limits or additional insured status
## Sums insured and inflation
Replacement costs move every year. Buildings, plant, stock, and business interruption gross profit figures should reflect current values — not the year the policy was first written.
- Obtain professional valuations for major property every 3 to 5 years
- Update stock declarations for peak and average seasons
- Review BI indemnity periods and standing charges after organisational change
- Adjust motor fleet values and hire-purchase interests on financed vehicles
## Claims history and near-misses

Insurers price renewal on loss experience. Present claims with context: recovered amounts, remedial actions, and open reserves. Near-misses (fires extinguished early, near collisions, cyber attempts) may justify cover improvements even if no claim was filed.
- Summarise claims by line: motor, property, liability, medical, WIBA
- Document corrective actions: training, alarms, maintenance, IT controls
- Challenge denials or partial settlements that should be appealed
## Board, lender, and contractual compliance

Loan covenants, lease agreements, government tenders, and international customer contracts often specify insurance wording. Collect certificates required for auditors and bankers in the renewal window — not after expiry.
- Match liability limits to contract tiers and tender requirements
- Confirm cross-liability and severability clauses where groups share policies
- Verify professional indemnity for consulting, engineering, or financial services arms
- Align D&O or management liability with governance changes
## Broker review meeting agenda

Book a structured renewal meeting with ADT at least 60 days before expiry. Bring finance, operations, and HR inputs — not only the insurance buyer. Walk away with a gap list, revised schedules, and a timeline for insurer submissions.

Renewing without this review is how corporates discover gaps during claims, not during renewal. Download the corporate pre-renewal PDF from our document centre or request a facilitated review session.

title: Claim document quality guide: what insurers expect on first submission
excerpt: Insurers approve files they can assess quickly: legible photos, consistent dates, matching amounts, and official reports in the right order. This guide explains the documentation standards ADT uses to pre-check claims before they reach the underwriter.
author: ADT Claims Desk
content: First-submission quality is the single biggest lever for claim speed. When documents are blurry, contradictory, or incomplete, assessors return the file — and each return adds days or weeks. This guide applies across motor, property, liability, medical, and WIBA claims, with line-specific notes where it matters.
## The facts sheet every file needs

Open with a half-page summary: policy number, insured name, incident date and time, location, brief description, estimated loss, and your contact details. Every other document should match these facts exactly.
- Use 24-hour time and East Africa Time where relevant
- State whether police, fire, hospital, or employer report exists
- List enclosures: photos (count), reports, estimates, invoices
- Name one contact for all insurer queries
## Photography and physical evidence standards
Phone photos are acceptable if they are clear and dated. Avoid heavy filters, extreme angles, or single close-ups without context shots.
- Wide shot showing entire asset or scene, then detail shots of each damaged area
- Include scale reference where helpful (ruler, familiar object)
- For theft: point of entry, ransacked areas, empty storage locations
- Do not dispose of damaged parts until the insurer or surveyor confirms
## Official reports and third-party documents
Motor claims often need a police abstract. Fire claims need brigade reports. WIBA claims need employer and medical documentation. Request reports promptly — delays here delay everything downstream.
- Verify names, dates, and registration numbers match your claim form
- Obtain certified copies where financiers or courts require them
- Translate foreign documents with a summary sheet if insurers request
## Financial documents: estimates, invoices, and proof of value

Repair estimates should itemise parts and labour. Stock losses need purchase invoices or stock records showing quantities on hand before the incident. Medical claims need itemised bills and discharge summaries.
- Match invoice dates to the incident timeline
- Explain any estimate variation before work starts
- Redact unrelated medical history while keeping diagnosis and treatment legible
## How ADT pre-checks your bundle

Send drafts to communications@adtinsurance.co.ke or WhatsApp the claims desk before formal submission. We flag gaps, suggest wording fixes, and route urgent files to insurer escalation contacts. A ten-minute pre-check often saves ten days of correspondence.
Download the claim reporting checklist from our document centre and keep a completed copy for every incident — even minor ones that may develop into larger losses later.

title: When to report a motor claim in Kenya: timing that protects your cover
excerpt: Notification windows in Kenyan motor policies are strict — and late reporting is one of the few reasons insurers can legitimately dispute a claim. Learn when to call, what to say on day one, and how to document delays you could not avoid.
author: ADT Motor Risk Team
content: Policy wording typically requires the insured to notify the insurer "immediately" or within a defined period after an accident, theft, or fire involving the vehicle. Kenyan courts and dispute mechanisms generally expect prompt reporting so the insurer can inspect damage, interview witnesses, and mitigate fraud. Timing is not a formality — it protects your right to indemnity.
## The first hour: safety, police, and photos

Attend to injuries first. Where the Road Traffic Act requires police attendance — serious injury, death, or significant damage — call the police before moving vehicles unless traffic authorities direct otherwise. Photograph the scene while layouts are intact.
- Switch on hazard lights and use triangles where required
- Exchange details with third parties without discussing fault
- Call your broker as soon as the scene is stable — even from the roadside
## The first 24 hours: formal notification

Most motor policies expect written or electronic notification within 24 to 48 hours. A WhatsApp message to your broker with photos and basic facts often satisfies initial notice while you complete the claim form.
- Record who you spoke to and at what time
- Keep the vehicle available for inspection unless towed for safety
- Report theft to police immediately and obtain an OB number the same day if possible
## When delay is unavoidable

Hospitalisation, remote accidents, or detention by authorities can delay reporting. If this applies, document dates, hospitals, or police stations involved and notify the broker with an explanation on the first day you are able.
- Retain medical admission records showing incapacity dates
- Ask a colleague to send initial photos and policy details on your behalf
- Do not authorise major repairs until the insurer or surveyor has sighted the vehicle unless emergency makes it impossible
## Theft, fire, and partial loss scenarios

Stolen vehicles must be reported to police without delay — insurers cross-check OB timing. Fire scenes should be preserved for investigation. For windscreen-only or minor parking damage, notification rules still apply even if you plan to self-fund below excess.
## ADT triage on WhatsApp and phone

The claims desk on +254 785 227 772 and your account advisor can confirm the exact window in your policy wording and log your initial notice. Early triage prevents the avoidable dispute that starts with "we were not informed in time."

title: WIBA claim documents: employer checklist for faster workforce injury filing
excerpt: Work injury claims fail when employee schedules are wrong, incident forms are late, or medical papers omit the work connection. Employers can cut WIBA filing time dramatically with this document checklist and a single internal owner.
author: ADT Compliance Desk
content: When an employee is injured at work, WIBA procedures require coordinated action from the site supervisor, HR, and management — often within tight reporting windows. Insurers pay valid claims quickly when the employer file is complete. Most delays we see are administrative: wrong employee on policy, missing medical nexus, or no DOSH notification where required.
## Before any injury: keep the policy schedule accurate
Prevention starts at renewal. Every employee engaged under a contract of service should appear on the WIBA schedule with correct ID, role, and commencement date.
- Reconcile payroll monthly against the insurer schedule
- Add new hires within the policy endorsement process — not at claim time
- Remove leavers promptly to avoid premium leakage
- Store the current certificate of insurance where site managers can access it
## At the time of injury: immediate steps

Provide first aid and arrange medical treatment. Record the time, exact location, task being performed, equipment involved, and witnesses. Serious injuries may require notification to the Directorate of Occupational Safety and Health Services (DOSH) — confirm thresholds with your safety advisor.
- Complete the employer incident report the same day
- Photograph the scene and equipment if safe to do so
- Obtain employee statement while facts are fresh
- Preserve CCTV or access logs where relevant
## Medical documentation employers must collect
Insurers need proof that treatment relates to a work injury. Ask the hospital for a clear diagnosis, treatment dates, and connection to the incident described on the employer form.
- Initial casualty or outpatient records
- Specialist referrals and discharge summaries
- Medical bills itemised by date and procedure
- Fit-for-work or return-to-work notes for rehabilitation planning
## Submission package for your broker
Send one bundle to ADT with a cover note listing enclosures. Include policy number, employee ID, incident summary, and HR contact.
- Completed insurer claim form and employer report
- Copy of employee ID and appointment letter if requested
- Witness statements and supervisor account
- DOSH notification acknowledgment if applicable
- Payslips or salary proof for benefit calculations where required
## After submission: stay the single point of contact

Insurers may request clarification on duty status, pre-existing conditions, or treatment necessity. Route all queries through one HR or safety lead in consultation with your broker to keep responses consistent.

title: Corporate insurance renewal timeline: 90, 60, and 30 days before expiry
excerpt: Corporate renewals compressed into the final week produce rushed endorsements, missed sub-limits, and premium surprises. This 90/60/30-day timeline gives CFOs and risk managers a practical calendar aligned to how insurers actually need information.
author: ADT Corporate Risk Desk
content: Large insurance programmes do not renew themselves. Insurers need updated exposure data, loss runs, and sometimes inspections before they quote. Starting late forces binary choices: accept terms as offered or risk lapses. A staged calendar spreads work across finance, operations, HR, and legal — and gives your broker time to market the programme properly.
## 90 days before expiry: exposure refresh
Pull the risk register, prior year claims bordereaux, and asset additions. This is the strategic review — what changed in the business and what should change in cover?
- Confirm renewal dates for every policy line (they may differ)
- List new entities, sites, products, and geographies
- Summarise open claims and reserves by line
- Capture board or audit recommendations touching insurance
- Brief ADT on mergers, divestitures, or capital projects in flight
## 60 days before expiry: values, limits, and contracts

Translate exposure changes into numbers: sums insured, liability limits, fleet schedules, headcount for WIBA and medical, marine annual sendings. Legal should flag contracts requiring certificate updates.
- Property and BI values vs current replacement and gross profit
- Liability limits vs largest contracts and tender requirements
- Motor fleet register with financier interests
- Medical census and benefit change requests from HR
- Cyber exposure review if IT footprint grew materially
## 30 days before expiry: quote comparison and gap closure
Receive draft quotes and schedules from insurers. Compare wording — not only premium. Exclusions, deductibles, and sub-limits moved in the last year are easy to miss in a spreadsheet of totals.
- Run a side-by-side on key clauses: flood, riot, cyber, professional indemnity
- Confirm no lapse in cover for high-risk activities
- Agree payment terms and debit note timing with finance
- Prepare board paper if governance requires approval above a threshold
## At renewal and immediately after
Issue certificates to lenders, landlords, and major clients. Update intranet contacts for claims and emergencies. Store signed schedules where site teams can access them.
- Distribute motor certificates and windscreen stickers to fleet managers
- Update WIBA and medical schedules with HR systems
- File proof of payment before cover activation deadlines
- Schedule a mid-term review if material projects launch before next renewal
## Who should attend each milestone

90-day call: CFO or finance lead, operations director, broker. 60-day: add HR for workforce lines, legal for contracts. 30-day: decision makers who can approve limits and premium. ADT facilitates these reviews for corporate clients across Kenya and cross-border programmes.
Use this timeline alongside our pre-renewal checklist article and downloadable corporate renewal PDF for a complete renewal toolkit.
